body.p: Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-145, and 147-151 were previously pending in this
application. Claim 149 has been amended. New claim 152 has been added. No new matter has been added.
Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-145, and 147-152 are pending for examination with claim
1 being independent.

Claim 149 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112 as allegedly being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.

Without acceding to the correctness of the rejection, claim 149 has been amended to recite that the adhesive comprises the polymer. Withdrawal of the claim rejection on this ground is respectfully requested.

Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-141, 147-149, and 151 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over U.S. Patent Publication No. 2010/0297686 to Gogotsi et al. ("Gogotsi") in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2013/0338627 to Rylander et al. ("Rylander").

The Patent Office alleges that Gogotsi teaches each and every feature of independent claim 1, except for: (i) an end portion having a substantially constant average cross-sectional diameter of less than 100 nm; (ii) the end portion having a length of between about 750 micrometers and about

3 mm; and (iii) a tapered portion having a length of no more than about 500 micrometers. Regarding (i), the Patent Office alleges that it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the diameter of the end portion of Gogotsi from about 100-150 nm to be less than 100 nm (see pages 6-7 of the Office Action). The Patent Office further alleges that (ii) and (iii) are taught by Rylander, and that it would have been obvious for a person of ordinary skill in the art to
combine Gogotsi and Rylander (see pages 7-8 of the Office Action). It is believed, however, that this rejection is deficient and should be withdrawn for at least the following reasons.

body.p: The Patent Office alleges that Gogotsi discloses a member comprising a tapered portion connecting the starting portion to the end portion (see page 5 of the Office Action), but concedes that Gogotsi fails to teach that the tapered portion has a length of no more than about 500 micrometers (see page 7 of the Office Action). The Patent Office further alleges that Rylander discloses a tapered portion having a length of no more than about 500 micrometers, that it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the length of the tapered portion of Gogotsi with the length of the tapered portion of Rylander, and that one of ordinary skill in the art would have had a reasonable expectation of success in doing so.

It is submitted that Gogotsi does not enable tapered portions having a length of no more than about 500 micrometers. This is because the technique taught in Gogotsi for producing tapered portions-the well-known technique of pulling glass capillaries-is incapable of producing tapered portions of such short dimensions. Instead, such techniques will result in tapered portions having tapers of several millimeters, not less than 500 micrometers.

For example, the acicular glass probes in Gogotsi are prepared by pulling a borosilicate glass capillary using a laser based micropipette puller from Sutter Instrument, USA (see paragraph [0070] of Gogotsi). As described in the instant specification, tapered portions having a length of 500 micrometers or less are difficult to achieve using such fabrication methods, which result in long (often meters) tapered portions instead (see, for example, page 7, lines 3-9 of the specification as filed). Furthermore, submitted herewith are instructions from Sutter Instrument, titled "Creating a Pipette with a Short Taper and a 25p to 35p Tip" ("Sutter"). Sutter describes that pulling glass creates a long (i.e., 5 mm to 10 mm) taper. Sutter also describes how to create a shorter (i.e., 3 mm to 4 mm) taper. The shorter tapers attainable by Sutter's instructions, however, are still 6-8 times

longer than the 500 micrometer maximum length of the tapered portion as recited in independent claim 1. Nowhere does Sutter teach or suggest how to make tapers of no more than about 500 micrometers, and one of ordinary skill of the art would not have been able to modify Sutter in such a fashion. To the contrary, techniques of pulling glass capillaries are incapable of producing tapered portions of such short dimensions.

In view of Gogotsi and Sutter, it is respectfully submitted that one of ordinary skill in the art seeking to modify the length of any tapered portion in Gogotsi with the length of the of the tapered portion in Rylander would not have had a reasonable expectation of success in doing so, as the glass pulling methods described in Gogotsi inherently result in micropipettes that include long tapered portions having a length of, at best, at least 3 mm. Shorter tapers are not taught in Gogosti, as Gogotsi teaches using the techniques described in Sutter, and are not enabled by Gogotsi in combination with Sutter. Instead, to decrease the length of any tapered portion in Gogotsi, one of ordinary skill in the art would have needed to use fabrication methods that do not rely on pulling glass capillaries, none of which are described or contemplated by Gogotsi.
I. Gogotsi fails to teach or render non-inventive: (i ) a member configured to guide and/or direct light; and (ii) at least one particle positioned in an optically interrogatable position

p.u: h the member to an end portion.

body.p: The Patent Office alleges that Gogotsi discloses a member configured to guide and/or direct light to analyze a cell (see pages 4-5 of the Office Action). The Patent Office further alleges that Gogotsi discloses at least one particle positioned in an optically interrogatable position with respect to light transmitted through the member to an end portion (see page 6 of the Office Action).

Gogotsi is generally directed to an acicular glass probe having a distal end surmounted by a population of metallic nanoparticles, wherein the distal end of the acicular glass probe is irradiated to obtain a surface-enhanced Raman signal (see, for example, paragraph [0005] of Gogotsi). Gogotsi describes that the SERS-active nanopipettes are inserted into a cell and continuously monitored under a Raman microscope. Gogotsi further describes that the excitation laser is focused on the nanopipette tip during data acquisition (see, for example, paragraphs [0049]-[0051] of

Gogotsi in conjunction with FIG. 11). As shown in FIG. 11 of Gogotsi, the excitation laser is mounted above the tip of the nanopipette such that the excitation light is directed on the tip of the nanopipette only, i.e., to excite the population of metallic nanoparticles surmounted thereon when the nanopipette tip is inserted into a cell.
Gogotsi therefore fails to teach or render non-inventive a member configured to guide

and/or direct light, as recited in independent claim 1. Instead, the nanopipette in Gogotsi merely functions as a probe that is inserted into the cell so that the metallic nanoparticles surmounted thereon can be irradiated by external excitation light that is not guided and/or directed in any way by the nanopipette. In addition, Gogotsi fails to teach or render non-inventive at least one particle positioned in an optically interrogatable position with respect to light transmitted through the member to an end portion. While Gogotsi teaches a population of metallic nanoparticles surmounted on a distal end of the acicular glass probe, there is no teaching or suggestion in Gogotsi that at least one of the metallic nanoparticles is positioned in an optically interrogatable position with respect to light transmitted through the member to the distal end of the glass probe.
Furthermore, paragraph [0099] in conjunction with FIG. 16b of Gogotsi describes that a

fiber optic-based SERS probe has not only a very large tip, but is also highly conical, and therefore is not optimal for cell probing and further shape optimization is required. Gogotsi therefore teaches away from a member configured to guide and/or direct light (see M.P.E.P. § 2145(X)(D)). The Patent Office is reminded that the prior art must be considered in its entirety, including disclosures that teach away from the claims (see M.P.E.P. § 2141.02(VI)). It is respectfully submitted that the dimensions of the member as recited in independent claim 1 obviate the issues identified in paragraph [0099] of Gogotsi, while also having the benefit of guiding and/or directing light through the member to analyze the cell (see, for example, page 7, lines 16-26 of the specification as filed).
III. Conclusion.
For at least the reasons outlined above, the combination of Gogotsi and Rylander does
render independent claim 1 obvious, and independent claim 1 is patentable over the combination of Gogotsi and Rylander. The remaining claims that stand rejected on this ground depend from

independent claim 1, and are therefore also patentable over the combinations of Gogotsi and Rylander for at least the reasons outlined above. In addition, it is not conceded that Gogotsi or Rylander, alone or in combination, teach or render obvious any of the features recited in claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-141, 147-149, and 151, as asserted by the Patent Office. Withdrawal of the claim rejections on this ground is respectfully requested.
New claim 152 has been added.
New claim 152 depends from independent claim 1, which is patentable over the cited

references for at least the reasons outlined above. Thus, new claim 152 is also patentable over the cited references for at least the reasons outlined above. In addition, new claim 152 recites features related to the member that further distinguish the cited references.
